blackIce.guidance:
# Black Ice: In-Car Reference Card

**WHAT IT IS:**
Black ice is a transparent layer of ice on road surfaces that looks like wet pavement, making it nearly invisible to drivers.

**ACTIONABLE STEPS:**

• **Reduce speed significantly** — Test the road surface with gentle braking to determine how slippery it is; drive at least 3–4 times slower than normal stopping distance would suggest

• **Increase following distance** — Maintain 5–6 seconds (or more) between your vehicle and the car ahead, versus the normal 3-second rule in summer

• **Avoid braking and steering inputs** — If you begin to skid, avoid sudden braking or abrupt turns; instead, disengage the clutch to regain traction, and steer gently to counteract rear-wheel skids

• **Be extra cautious on bridges, overpasses, and ramps** — Black ice forms first on these elevated structures since air circulates above and below, causing rapid temperature drops

compactedSnow.guidance:
# Driving on Compacted Snow

**What it is:** Compacted snow requires reduced speed, increased following distance, and gentle vehicle control to maintain traction.

• **Tyres:** Use winter tires (especially Nordic-type studded or unstudded) with adequate tread depth; narrow tires perform better on snow than wide tires

• **Speed:** Reduce speed significantly and test the surface frequently with gentle braking to know how slippery it is; corner at less than 30 km/h (18 mph)

• **Braking:** Avoid hard braking; use gentle braking to test conditions; on downhill stretches, downshift to reduce speed rather than brake, as braking can cause the vehicle to fishtail

• **Distance:** Increase following distance from the standard 3 seconds to 5–6 seconds or more behind the vehicle ahead

slush.guidance:
# Slush (Melting/Mixed Snow): Aquaplaning-Like Risk

**Slush is soft, melting snow that is more slippery than ice and presents aquaplaning-like hazards due to reduced handling and traction.**

• **Reduce speed significantly** — Steering (handling) is particularly difficult on slush; approach at cautious speeds and test braking gently to assess surface grip

• **Avoid sudden maneuvers** — Do not make sharp turns or hard acceleration/braking; any abrupt control input risks loss of traction similar to aquaplaning

• **Increase following distance** — Maintain 5–6 seconds (or more) behind the vehicle ahead, as braking distance increases dramatically on slush

• **Stay in plowed/traveled lanes** — Keep to the main traffic path where the surface has been compacted; avoid moving suddenly across uncleared slush between lanes, as it can "grab" a wheel with disastrous consequences

wet.guidance:
# Avoiding Aquaplaning and Loss of Grip on Wet Roads

**Reduce speed and increase following distance to maintain control on slippery surfaces.**

• **Slow down significantly** — Reduce your speed well below normal; aquaplaning typically begins above 72–93 km/h (45–58 mph), so slower speeds give tires time to disperse water

• **Increase distance to the car ahead** — Extend your following distance from the standard 3 seconds to 5–6 seconds or more to allow extra stopping distance on wet pavement

• **Avoid sudden steering or braking inputs** — Make smooth, gradual control adjustments; sudden maneuvers or hard braking can trigger loss of traction or skidding

• **Do not use cruise control** — Maintain manual speed control to respond smoothly to changing road conditions and pooled water
